newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Bhutto says she's in danger after brother's death.
newsitem.headline: Bhutto says she's in danger after brother's death.

text.p: Pakistani Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto was quoted on Saturday as saying she did not feel safe after what she called the political murder of her estranged younger brother Murtaza Bhutto.

She told the Pakistani daily The News she did not believe a police report that Murtaza was killed in crossfire between police and his guards on September 20. She said her government sought British experts to help find out what really happened.
"I don't know who is the next," Bhutto said. "I don't feel safe any more. My husband and my children are not safe."
Bhutto called Murtaza's killing a conpiracy against her family, party and government and said she was determined to unearth it despite personal risk.

"It seems that the Bhuttos are meant to be killed," she said, referring to the execution of her father Zulfikar Ali Bhutto in 1979 after being deposed as prime minister in a 1977 army coup as well as the 1985 death of her youngest brother Shahnawaz in his flat in southern France in still unexplained circumstances.

Apparently referring to critics who blamed her government for Murtaza's killing, she said she felt a situation had been created similar to that in the port city of Karachi where rival ethnic groups are accused of killing each other's militants.
"I am a politician, an educated person, I know history, and I feel there is more to this," she said.
"I don't know whether they are going to hit me next, my husband next, hit my children next, and God forbid they are going to hit my mother, Murtaza's children next and other members of my family."
Murtaza, 42, and seven activists of his Shaheed Bhutto faction of the ruling Pakistan People's Party (PPP), were killed on the night of September 20 in Karachi's affluent seaside Clifton district.
Police said Murtaza was killed in the crossfire when police retaliated in self-defence after his followers opened fire and injured two police officers and a cab driver.
"I don't believe the story of the cross-fire," Bhutto said.
She wondered why there was a delay in taking Murtaza to hospital and one that lacked appropriate facilities.

"Why did they let my brother bleed on the street, in the hospital, and bleed and bleed. Why did they bleed him to death. Why didn't they say that they didn't have the doctors, a blood unit and an emergency care."

Bhutto said although Murtaza had formed a rival political group, she always thought that if something happened to her, people would turn to him to carry forward his father's "mission and dream of a Pakistan which is democratic, federal, egalitarian and progressive.
"After his brutal death, I feel absolutely isolated," she said.
